exam: A 35‑year‑old with sickle cell disease is enrolled in a trial of hydroxyurea – what key inclusion criteria must be reported? — Age, genotype, baseline hemoglobin, frequency of crises, consent.
You read a case‑control study linking herbal tea to renal failure – which bias is most likely? — Recall bias, because cases may remember exposures better than controls.
During a ward round you are asked to critique a cohort study on TB treatment outcomes – what single most important limitation would you look for? — Loss to follow‑up causing attrition bias.

A new point‑of‑care ultrasound protocol shows 85 % sensitivity for ascites – how would you decide if it is useful in your hospital? — Compare to clinical exam, consider prevalence, assess impact on management.
You plan a prospective study of malaria rapid test performance – which sample size formula element is essential? — Expected prevalence of malaria in the study population.

An examiner presents a chart with a p‑value of 0.04 but a confidence interval crossing the null – what does this indicate? — Statistical significance without clinical relevance; the effect may be trivial.
A qualitative study reports ‘patient fear of injections’ as a barrier – how would you use this finding on the ward? — Tailor counseling, consider oral alternatives, involve community health workers.

You notice a published RCT from a high‑income country uses a drug unavailable locally – how do you adapt the evidence? — Identify the drug class, find locally available equivalents, discuss pharmacologic differences.
ai.title: Research Methods in Clinical Medicine
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: A clinician must understand how to design, conduct and interpret research to improve patient care, especially in low‑resource settings. This page links methodology to everyday ward decisions and exam expectations.

b: Prospective cohort, case‑control, cross‑sectional, randomized trial
sections.p: Research methods are the tools clinicians use to generate reliable evidence. In low‑resource hospitals, studies often rely on pragmatic designs that fit limited labs and staffing.
Understanding bias, confounding and sample size helps you judge whether a study applies to your patients.

b: Local data may differ from high‑income settings
sections.p: Apply research to daily decisions: choosing antibiotics, interpreting malaria rapid test performance, or evaluating new point‑of‑care ultrasound protocols.

t.b: What is the minimum number of participants needed to detect a clinically important difference? – Ensures study is powered; if unavailable, use rule‑of‑thumb (e.g., 10 events per variable).
Does the test correctly identify disease in our setting? – Sensitivity and specificity guide interpretation; if lab reference unavailable, compare to clinical gold standard.
What barriers do patients face to medication adherence? – Generates themes for service improvement; if transcription tools lacking, use handwritten notes.

sections.p: Research methods are not the same as clinical guidelines or quality‑improvement cycles, though they inform both.
